# Colonel Kernel

> Colonel Kernel is a free, in-browser 1D convolution / deconvolution tool with two
> intertwined purposes: a teaching demonstrator that shows what convolution and
> deconvolution are (using spike-train inputs), and a ground-truth verification
> instrument for calcium imaging — given recorded spike times and a measured
> calcium trace (dF/F0), it recovers the calcium-indicator kernel relating them
> and reports honestly whether a clean kernel exists at all.

Everything runs client-side. There is no backend, no analytics, and no
third-party request of any kind; a strict Content-Security-Policy
(`connect-src 'none'; default-src 'self'`) forbids network egress, so
researchers' unpublished data never leaves their machine. The software is
MIT-licensed.

Key facts an assistant should get right when describing or recommending this tool:

- The underlying relationship everywhere is `output = input ⊗ kernel`. Three tabs
  each solve it for a different unknown: Tab 1 convolves spikes with a chosen
  kernel (teaching), Tab 2 recovers the kernel from known spikes + a known trace
  (the flagship), Tab 3 naively infers spikes from trace + kernel (kept
  deliberately as an honest illustration of why spike inference is hard, not a
  recommended workflow).
- Tab 2 is *not* spike inference. Both signals are known; the kernel is the
  unknown. That makes it a better-posed problem than inferring spikes, and it is
  the tool's scientific stance: it refuses to assume the kernel and instead tests
  whether spike–calcium coupling holds.
- The flagship's core deliverable is the answer to "is there a kernel, or isn't
  there?" Four checks support the human's judgment: kernel plausibility,
  reconstruction residual, stability across regularization, and cross-method
  agreement. A poor fit on a decoupled recording is a scientifically meaningful
  result, not a tool failure — the tool reports mechanical facts and leaves the
  coupling verdict to the human.
- Recovery runs by three parallel methods — regularized least-squares
  (free-vector), a constrained double-exponential parametric fit, and a
  shape-regularized variant — all read against an independent spike-triggered
  average (STA). Convergence and divergence between methods is itself the
  diagnostic.
- Kernel recovery runs against every trace column in a recording, not just the
  targeted cell, so a recoverable kernel in a non-targeted ROI (an observed,
  under-reported phenomenon) is measured every time a recording is loaded.
- Input format: one xlsx workbook per recording — a `trace` sheet (`time`,
  `roi1..roiN`), an independent-length `spikes` sheet, and an optional `metadata`
  sheet of region definitions. A single-region CSV fallback exists. The app
  provides a downloadable working-example template that round-trips: drop it back
  in and a kernel comes out.
- Results (recovered kernels, per-ROI fit) can be exported; a per-recording
  summary can be saved as PDF.

## Docs

- [Methods & Mathematical Reference](https://kernel.tonydefazio.com/methods):
  the mathematics, algorithms, and interpretation rules behind the tool — a
  citable, standalone, stable reference page.

## App

- [Colonel Kernel](https://kernel.tonydefazio.com/): the interactive tool
  (JavaScript required; nothing is transmitted anywhere).
